content.text:
# Production-Grade LSTM Financial Price Prediction: Quantitative Best Practices

I will provide a comprehensive advisory drawing on established quantitative finance methodology and current best practices. Let me structure this systematically across all eight of your questions.

---

## 1. Quant-Specific Libraries and Technology Stack

### Core Deep Learning

| Library | Role | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **PyTorch** (preferred) | Model development | Dominant in quant research; dynamic graphs enable custom architectures; better debugging than TF/Keras |
| **PyTorch Lightning** | Training orchestration | Eliminates boilerplate; built-in logging, checkpointing, early stopping |
| **PyTorch Forecasting** | Time series models | Production-ready temporal fusion transformers, DeepAR, N-BEATS alongside LSTM baselines |

### Quant-Specific Frameworks

| Library | What It Does | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Microsoft Qlib** | End-to-end quant research platform | Alpha factor mining, model training, backtesting in one framework. Has LSTM/GRU built in. Strong walk-forward support. |
| **FinRL** | Reinforcement learning for finance | Useful if you extend beyond supervised prediction to execution/allocation |
| **VectorBT** | Vectorized backtesting | Extremely fast backtesting of signals generated by your models; supports walk-forward |
| **Zipline-Reloaded / Backtrader** | Event-driven backtesting | More realistic for slippage/commission modeling |
| **QuantStats** | Performance analytics | Generates tear sheets with Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, drawdown, rolling metrics -- one function call |
| **arch** (Kevin Sheppard) | GARCH/volatility modeling | Volatility normalization, regime detection via conditional variance |
| **statsmodels** | Statistical testing | ADF, KPSS, Ljung-Box, Engle-Granger, Johansen -- all the stationarity and serial correlation tests |

### Data and Feature Engineering

| Library | Role |
|---|---|
| **TA-Lib** or **pandas-ta** | Technical indicator computation (RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, etc.) |
| **tsfresh** | Automated time series feature extraction |
| **yfinance / ccxt / MetaTrader5** | Data acquisition for equities, crypto, forex respectively |
| **polars** | High-performance dataframe operations for large tick datasets |

### Infrastructure

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| **MLflow** or **Weights & Biases** | Experiment tracking, model registry, hyperparameter logging |
| **Optuna** | Bayesian hyperparameter optimization (far superior to grid search for LSTM tuning) |
| **DVC** | Data version control -- critical when your training windows shift in walk-forward |

### Recommended Stack Summary

```
Data:       ccxt + MT5 + polars + pandas-ta
Features:   tsfresh + pandas-ta + custom rolling statistics
Modeling:   PyTorch + PyTorch Lightning
Validation: Walk-forward custom code + VectorBT for signal backtesting
Analytics:  QuantStats + statsmodels + arch
Tracking:   MLflow or W&B + Optuna
```

---

## 2. Financial Metrics That Actually Matter

Standard ML metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE) are necessary but woefully insufficient. Quants evaluate models through the lens of tradability.

### Tier 1: Must-Have Metrics

| Metric | Formula / Definition | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharpe Ratio** | (E[R] - Rf) / std(R), annualized | > 1.5 for viable strategy; > 2.0 is strong |
| **Sortino Ratio** | (E[R] - Rf) / downside_std(R) | > 2.0; penalizes only downside vol |
| **Maximum Drawdown** | Largest peak-to-trough decline | < 15-20% for most allocators |
| **Calmar Ratio** | Annualized return / Max drawdown | > 1.0; measures return per unit of drawdown pain |
| **Hit Ratio (Accuracy)** | % of correct directional predictions | > 53% for viable trading at typical reward/risk |
| **Profit Factor** | Gross profits / Gross losses | > 1.5 |
| **Annualized Return** | Geometric mean return, annualized | Context-dependent |

### Tier 2: Professional Differentiation

| Metric | Why It Matters |
|---|---|
| **Information Ratio** | Alpha per unit of tracking error vs benchmark (buy-and-hold) |
| **Omega Ratio** | Probability-weighted ratio of gains to losses at a threshold; captures full return distribution |
| **Tail Ratio** | 95th percentile return / abs(5th percentile return); measures asymmetry of tails |
| **Average Win / Average Loss** | Combined with hit ratio, determines if the strategy is viable |
| **Expected Shortfall (CVaR)** | Average loss in the worst X% of cases; more informative than VaR |
| **Recovery Factor** | Net profit / Max drawdown; how quickly you recover |
| **Ulcer Index** | Duration-weighted drawdown measure |
| **Turnover** | How frequently positions change; impacts transaction costs |

### Tier 3: Statistical Rigor

| Test / Metric | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Diebold-Mariano Test** | Statistically compare forecast accuracy between your models and baselines |
| **Model Confidence Set (MCS)** | Hansen's MCS identifies the set of models with statistically equivalent performance |
| **T-statistic of Returns** | Is your mean return statistically different from zero? t > 2.0 at minimum |
| **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** | Harvey and Liu (2015) adjustment for multiple testing; critical when comparing 5 model variants |
| **Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO)** | Bailey et al. -- measures likelihood that your best model is overfit |

### Key Principle

Never report a Sharpe ratio without reporting the t-statistic of that Sharpe. A Sharpe of 2.0 over 6 months of daily data has a t-stat of approximately 1.0 -- statistically indistinguishable from zero. You need years of data or out-of-sample confirmation.

---

## 3. Critical Preprocessing for Financial Time Series

### Stationarity Pipeline

Financial prices are non-stationary (unit root processes). You must transform them.

```
Raw Prices
    |
    v
Log Returns: r_t = ln(P_t / P_{t-1})
    |
    v
Stationarity Test (ADF + KPSS jointly)
    |
    v
If non-stationary: further differencing or fractional differencing
    |
    v
Volatility Normalization
    |
    v
Feature Scaling (per walk-forward window)
```

### Specific Steps

**A. Returns Computation (see Question 5 for details)**
- Use log-returns for the target variable
- For features, both raw and normalized forms may be useful

**B. Stationarity Testing**
- Apply ADF test (null: unit root exists) AND KPSS test (null: stationary) jointly
- If ADF rejects but KPSS does not reject: stationary
- If both reject or neither rejects: fractionally differenced (see Marcos Lopez de Prado's approach)

**C. Volatility Normalization**
This is arguably the most important preprocessing step for financial ML.

```python
# Normalize returns by rolling volatility
normalized_return = return_t / rolling_std(returns, window=20)

# Or use GARCH-normalized returns
from arch import arch_model
garch = arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1)
result = garch.fit(disp='off')
standardized = returns / result.conditional_volatility
```

Why: A 1% move in gold during low-vol environments is a very different signal than 1% during high-vol. Without normalization, your LSTM learns a muddled mapping.

**D. Feature Scaling -- Walk-Forward Safe**

```python
# WRONG: fit scaler on entire dataset (look-ahead bias)
scaler.fit(all_data)

# CORRECT: fit scaler only on training window, transform test
scaler.fit(train_window)
train_scaled = scaler.transform(train_window)
test_scaled = scaler.transform(test_window)
```

Use `RobustScaler` (median/IQR) rather than `StandardScaler` (mean/std) -- financial data has fat tails and outliers that distort mean/std.

**E. Outlier Treatment**
- Winsorize at 3-sigma or use IQR-based capping
- Do NOT remove outliers -- they contain real market information (flash crashes, news events)
- Cap them to reduce undue influence on gradient updates

**F. Missing Data**
- Forward-fill is standard for financial data (last known price persists)
- Never interpolate -- it creates look-ahead bias
- Mark gaps explicitly (e.g., weekend gaps in forex with a binary feature)

**G. Feature Engineering -- Quant-Grade**

Essential features for LSTM input:

```
Returns:           log_return, abs_return (realized vol proxy)
Volatility:        ATR, Bollinger Band width, Garman-Klass vol, Parkinson vol
Momentum:          RSI(14), MACD, ROC(various periods)
Mean Reversion:    z-score of price vs moving average
Microstructure:    bid-ask spread (if available), volume profile
Calendar:          hour_of_day, day_of_week, month (cyclical encoding)
Cross-asset:       DXY for gold/forex, VIX for all, US10Y yield
Regime:            rolling Hurst exponent, rolling autocorrelation
```

---

## 4. Common Pitfalls in Financial ML

### Critical Errors (Will Invalidate Results)

| Pitfall | Description | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Look-ahead bias** | Using future information in training features or scaling | Strict temporal ordering; walk-forward only; no global normalization |
| **Information leakage in sequences** | Overlapping sequences where test sequences contain training data points | Ensure gap between train and test equal to sequence length |
| **Fitting on the full dataset** | Any preprocessing (PCA, feature selection, scaling) on full data | All fitting must occur within each walk-forward training window |
| **Overfitting to backtest** | Optimizing hyperparameters on the same data you report results on | Three-way split: train / validation / test; or nested walk-forward |
| **Survivorship bias** | Only including instruments that still exist | Less relevant for XAUUSD/EURUSD/BTCUSD specifically, but critical for stock universes |

### Methodological Errors (Will Produce Misleading Results)

| Pitfall | Description | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-stationarity ignored** | Training on raw prices | Use returns or stationary transformations |
| **Ignoring transaction costs** | Reporting gross returns | Model spread, commission, slippage explicitly; use realistic estimates (2-3 pips for EURUSD, $0.30-0.50 for gold, 0.1% for BTC) |
| **Ignoring market impact** | Assuming infinite liquidity | Not critical for small capital, but note it |
| **Regime non-stationarity** | Model trained in trending regime, tested in ranging | Include regime detection; report performance by regime |
| **Multiple testing bias** | Comparing 5 models and picking the best without correction | Apply Bonferroni or use Deflated Sharpe Ratio / PBO |
| **Sequence length sensitivity** | Arbitrarily choosing lookback window | Treat it as a hyperparameter; optimize via Optuna |
| **Target leakage via technical indicators** | Some indicators use future bars in their smoothing | Verify every indicator is causal (uses only past data) |

### Practical Errors (Will Cause Production Failures)

| Pitfall | Description |
|---|---|
| **Training/serving skew** | Feature computation differs between training and live inference |
| **Concept drift** | Model degrades as market dynamics change; must have retraining schedule |
| **Gradient issues** | LSTMs suffer from vanishing gradients on very long sequences; keep sequence length reasonable (50-200 for hourly, 30-90 for daily) |
| **Class imbalance** | If predicting direction, markets are roughly 50/50 but not exactly; use stratified sampling |

---

## 5. Returns vs Prices as Targets

### Definitive Answer: Use Log-Returns

**Never use raw prices as the prediction target.** Here is why:

| Criterion | Raw Prices | Simple Returns | Log Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stationarity | Non-stationary | Approximately stationary | Approximately stationary |
| Additivity | N/A | Not time-additive | Time-additive: sum of log returns = log return of period |
| Normality | Not normal | Approximately normal for short horizons | Slightly better normality properties |
| Symmetry | N/A | Asymmetric (-100% floor, no ceiling) | Symmetric |
| Small moves | N/A | r and ln(1+r) nearly identical | Equivalent for small moves |
| Compounding | N/A | Must be compounded multiplicatively | Sum directly for multi-period returns |
| Neural network training | Poor gradient behavior; scale changes over time | Good | Best |

### Practical Implementation

```python
# Target variable
log_return = np.log(close_t / close_{t-1})

# For multi-step ahead prediction (e.g., predict next 5 bars cumulative)
cumulative_log_return = np.log(close_{t+5} / close_t)
# This equals sum of individual log returns -- clean and additive

# Converting predictions back to prices
predicted_price = current_price * np.exp(predicted_log_return)
```

### When Simple Returns Are Acceptable

- For portfolio-level aggregation (cross-sectional returns of multiple assets are additive in simple return space, not log return space)
- When the audience/reporting requires it

### Classification Alternative

Many professional quant shops frame this as a classification problem:

```
Class +1:  next-bar log return > +threshold
Class  0:  abs(next-bar log return) <= threshold  (no-trade zone)
Class -1:  next-bar log return < -threshold
```

Where `threshold` is calibrated to transaction costs. This directly maps to a trading signal and avoids the problem of optimizing for point-estimate accuracy when all you need is direction.

---

## 6. Statistical Tests to Include

### Pre-Modeling Tests (Data Quality and Assumptions)

| Test | Null Hypothesis | Purpose | Library |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF)** | Series has unit root | Confirm returns are stationary | `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.adfuller` |
| **KPSS** | Series is stationary | Use jointly with ADF for robust conclusion | `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.kpss` |
| **Phillips-Perron** | Series has unit root | More robust to heteroskedasticity than ADF | `arch.unitroot.PhillipsPerron` |
| **Ljung-Box** | No autocorrelation up to lag k | Check if returns have predictable structure | `statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.acorr_ljungbox` |
| **ARCH-LM** | No ARCH effects | Confirm volatility clustering exists (justifies vol normalization) | `statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_arch` |
| **Jarque-Bera** | Returns are normally distributed | Quantify fat tails; will almost always reject for financial data | `scipy.stats.jarque_bera` |
| **Hurst Exponent** | H=0.5 (random walk) | H>0.5 suggests trending; H<0.5 suggests mean-reverting | Custom or `hurst` package |

### Model Evaluation Tests

| Test | Purpose | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Diebold-Mariano (DM)** | Compare predictive accuracy of two models | Pairwise comparison of your 5 model variants |
| **Model Confidence Set (MCS)** | Identify set of statistically equivalent best models | After running all 5 variants |
| **Giacomini-White** | Conditional predictive ability test; accounts for estimation uncertainty | More powerful than DM for nested models |
| **Mincer-Zarnowitz Regression** | Regress realized values on forecasts; test intercept=0, slope=1 | Forecast calibration check |
| **Pesaran-Timmermann (PT)** | Test directional accuracy | Is directional prediction better than chance? |

### Post-Modeling / Strategy Tests

| Test | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Bootstrap Sharpe Ratio CI** | Confidence interval on Sharpe; use circular block bootstrap to preserve autocorrelation |
| **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** | Adjusts for multiple comparisons across your 5 models |
| **White's Reality Check / SPA** | Tests if best strategy is significantly better than benchmark after data snooping adjustment |
| **CUSUM Test** | Detect structural breaks in model residuals over time |
| **Chow Test** | Test for regime breaks at known dates (e.g., COVID crash, rate hike cycles) |

---

## 7. Handling Market Regimes

### Why Regimes Matter

An LSTM trained predominantly in trending markets will fail catastrophically in ranging markets, and vice versa. Gold in 2020-2024 exhibited at least three distinct regimes (COVID flight-to-safety, post-COVID consolidation, 2024 breakout). BTCUSD has historically alternated between explosive trending and extended drawdown regimes.

### Regime Detection Methods

**A. Hidden Markov Models (HMM) -- Most Common in Quant Finance**

```python
from hmmlearn import GaussianHMM

# Fit 2-3 state HMM on returns + volatility
model = GaussianHMM(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", n_iter=100)
features = np.column_stack([returns, rolling_vol])
model.fit(features)
regimes = model.predict(features)
# States typically map to: low-vol trending, high-vol trending, ranging
```

**B. Rolling Hurst Exponent**

```
H > 0.6:  Trending regime  -> momentum strategies / trend-following signals
H ~ 0.5:  Random walk      -> reduce position size / go flat
H < 0.4:  Mean-reverting   -> mean-reversion signals
```

**C. Volatility Regime via GARCH or Simple Thresholds**

```
Low vol:    rolling_vol < 25th percentile of historical
Normal vol: 25th-75th percentile
High vol:   > 75th percentile
Crisis:     > 95th percentile
```

### Integration Strategies

**Option 1: Regime as Input Feature (Simplest)**
- Add regime label as a feature to LSTM input
- Model learns to condition predictions on regime
- Risk: regime detection itself may have lag

**Option 2: Regime-Specific Models (Most Robust)**
- Train separate LSTMs per regime
- Use regime detector as a routing layer
- Report performance per regime separately
- Challenge: less training data per regime

**Option 3: Regime-Aware Position Sizing (Pragmatic)**
- Single model for prediction
- Scale position size inversely with volatility regime
- Reduce or eliminate positions during regime transitions (high uncertainty)

**Option 4: Mixture of Experts**
- Train a gating network that learns to weight regime-specific expert models
- More complex but theoretically elegant

### Recommendation for Your Setup

Use Option 1 (regime as feature) combined with Option 3 (regime-aware sizing) and always report metrics broken down by regime in your results.

```
Overall Sharpe: 1.8
  - Trending regime:   2.4  (model excels)
  - Ranging regime:    0.9  (model struggles)
  - High-vol regime:   1.5  (adequate)
```

This level of transparency is what distinguishes professional quant reports from academic exercises.

---

## 8. What Makes a Financial ML Report Professional / Production-Grade

### Report Structure

```
1. Executive Summary
   - Strategy thesis in 2-3 sentences
   - Key metrics table (Sharpe, Max DD, Annual Return, Hit Ratio)
   - Investment recommendation

2. Data Description
   - Instruments, timeframes, date ranges
   - Data source and quality assessment
   - Summary statistics table (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, ADF p-value)
   - Return distribution plots with normal overlay

3. Feature Engineering
   - Complete feature list with economic rationale for each
   - Stationarity test results for all features
   - Correlation matrix / VIF for multicollinearity assessment

4. Methodology
   - Model architectures with layer dimensions
   - Walk-forward validation design (diagram)
   - Training protocol (optimizer, learning rate schedule, early stopping)
   - Hyperparameter optimization approach

5. Results
   - Per-model performance table (all metrics from Section 2)
   - Statistical significance tests (DM, MCS, Deflated Sharpe)
   - Equity curves with drawdown overlay
   - Performance by regime
   - Performance by year (vintage analysis)
   - Rolling Sharpe ratio plot (12-month window)
   - Monthly returns heatmap

6. Risk Analysis
   - Drawdown analysis (top 5 drawdowns with dates and recovery time)
   - VaR and CVaR at 95% and 99%
   - Stress test results (COVID crash, 2022 rate hikes, etc.)
   - Correlation with benchmark during stress periods

7. Robustness Checks
   - Sensitivity to hyperparameters
   - Performance with different lookback windows
   - Performance with perturbed entry/exit thresholds
   - Out-of-sample degradation analysis

8. Limitations and Risks
   - Known failure modes
   - Regime dependencies
   - Data limitations
   - Model decay expectations

9. Appendix
   - Full hyperparameter tables
   - All statistical test outputs
   - Code repository reference
```

### Visual Standards

| Chart | Purpose | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Cumulative returns vs buy-and-hold | Strategy value-add at a glance | matplotlib / plotly |
| Underwater (drawdown) plot | Risk visualization | QuantStats |
| Monthly returns heatmap | Seasonality and consistency | seaborn / QuantStats |

### What Separates Amateur from Professional

| Amateur | Professional |

| Reports MSE only | Reports Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, max DD, hit ratio, profit factor |
| Single train/test split | Walk-forward with multiple windows |


2. Aggregate out-of-sample predictions across all windows
3. Compute all metrics on aggregated OOS predictions
4. Run pairwise Diebold-Mariano tests
5. Compute Model Confidence Set
6. Apply Deflated Sharpe Ratio to the winner
7. Report ALL models' results, not just the best one

A model that achieves a Sharpe of 1.2 honestly out-of-sample, with proper walk-forward validation, realistic transaction costs, and statistical significance, is worth far more than one that claims 3.0 on a cherry-picked backtest. # Production-Grade LSTM Financial Price Prediction: Quantitative Best Practices

I will provide a comprehensive advisory drawing on established quantitative finance methodology and current best practices. Let me structure this systematically across all eight of your questions.

---

## 1. Quant-Specific Libraries and Technology Stack

### Core Deep Learning

| Library | Role | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **PyTorch** (preferred) | Model development | Dominant in quant research; dynamic graphs enable custom architectures; better debugging than TF/Keras |
| **PyTorch Lightning** | Training orchestration | Eliminates boilerplate; built-in logging, checkpointing, early stopping |
| **PyTorch Forecasting** | Time series models | Production-ready temporal fusion transformers, DeepAR, N-BEATS alongside LSTM baselines |

### Quant-Specific Frameworks

| Library | What It Does | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Microsoft Qlib** | End-to-end quant research platform | Alpha factor mining, model training, backtesting in one framework. Has LSTM/GRU built in. Strong walk-forward support. |
| **FinRL** | Reinforcement learning for finance | Useful if you extend beyond supervised prediction to execution/allocation |
| **VectorBT** | Vectorized backtesting | Extremely fast backtesting of signals generated by your models; supports walk-forward |
| **Zipline-Reloaded / Backtrader** | Event-driven backtesting | More realistic for slippage/commission modeling |
| **QuantStats** | Performance analytics | Generates tear sheets with Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, drawdown, rolling metrics -- one function call |
| **arch** (Kevin Sheppard) | GARCH/volatility modeling | Volatility normalization, regime detection via conditional variance |
| **statsmodels** | Statistical testing | ADF, KPSS, Ljung-Box, Engle-Granger, Johansen -- all the stationarity and serial correlation tests |

### Data and Feature Engineering

| Library | Role |
|---|---|
| **TA-Lib** or **pandas-ta** | Technical indicator computation (RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, etc.) |
| **tsfresh** | Automated time series feature extraction |
| **yfinance / ccxt / MetaTrader5** | Data acquisition for equities, crypto, forex respectively |
| **polars** | High-performance dataframe operations for large tick datasets |

### Infrastructure

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| **MLflow** or **Weights & Biases** | Experiment tracking, model registry, hyperparameter logging |
| **Optuna** | Bayesian hyperparameter optimization (far superior to grid search for LSTM tuning) |
| **DVC** | Data version control -- critical when your training windows shift in walk-forward |

### Recommended Stack Summary

```
Data:       ccxt + MT5 + polars + pandas-ta
Features:   tsfresh + pandas-ta + custom rolling statistics
Modeling:   PyTorch + PyTorch Lightning
Validation: Walk-forward custom code + VectorBT for signal backtesting
Analytics:  QuantStats + statsmodels + arch
Tracking:   MLflow or W&B + Optuna
```

---

## 2. Financial Metrics That Actually Matter

Standard ML metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE) are necessary but woefully insufficient. Quants evaluate models through the lens of tradability.

### Tier 1: Must-Have Metrics

| Metric | Formula / Definition | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharpe Ratio** | (E[R] - Rf) / std(R), annualized | > 1.5 for viable strategy; > 2.0 is strong |
| **Sortino Ratio** | (E[R] - Rf) / downside_std(R) | > 2.0; penalizes only downside vol |
| **Maximum Drawdown** | Largest peak-to-trough decline | < 15-20% for most allocators |
| **Calmar Ratio** | Annualized return / Max drawdown | > 1.0; measures return per unit of drawdown pain |
| **Hit Ratio (Accuracy)** | % of correct directional predictions | > 53% for viable trading at typical reward/risk |
| **Profit Factor** | Gross profits / Gross losses | > 1.5 |
| **Annualized Return** | Geometric mean return, annualized | Context-dependent |

### Tier 2: Professional Differentiation

| Metric | Why It Matters |
|---|---|
| **Information Ratio** | Alpha per unit of tracking error vs benchmark (buy-and-hold) |
| **Omega Ratio** | Probability-weighted ratio of gains to losses at a threshold; captures full return distribution |
| **Tail Ratio** | 95th percentile return / abs(5th percentile return); measures asymmetry of tails |
| **Average Win / Average Loss** | Combined with hit ratio, determines if the strategy is viable |
| **Expected Shortfall (CVaR)** | Average loss in the worst X% of cases; more informative than VaR |
| **Recovery Factor** | Net profit / Max drawdown; how quickly you recover |
| **Ulcer Index** | Duration-weighted drawdown measure |
| **Turnover** | How frequently positions change; impacts transaction costs |

### Tier 3: Statistical Rigor

| Test / Metric | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Diebold-Mariano Test** | Statistically compare forecast accuracy between your models and baselines |
| **Model Confidence Set (MCS)** | Hansen's MCS identifies the set of models with statistically equivalent performance |
| **T-statistic of Returns** | Is your mean return statistically different from zero? t > 2.0 at minimum |
| **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** | Harvey and Liu (2015) adjustment for multiple testing; critical when comparing 5 model variants |
| **Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO)** | Bailey et al. -- measures likelihood that your best model is overfit |

### Key Principle

Never report a Sharpe ratio without reporting the t-statistic of that Sharpe. A Sharpe of 2.0 over 6 months of daily data has a t-stat of approximately 1.0 -- statistically indistinguishable from zero. You need years of data or out-of-sample confirmation.

---

## 3. Critical Preprocessing for Financial Time Series

### Stationarity Pipeline

Financial prices are non-stationary (unit root processes). You must transform them.

```
Raw Prices
    |
    v
Log Returns: r_t = ln(P_t / P_{t-1})
    |
    v
Stationarity Test (ADF + KPSS jointly)
    |
    v
If non-stationary: further differencing or fractional differencing
    |
    v
Volatility Normalization
    |
    v
Feature Scaling (per walk-forward window)
```

### Specific Steps

**A. Returns Computation (see Question 5 for details)**
- Use log-returns for the target variable
- For features, both raw and normalized forms may be useful

**B. Stationarity Testing**
- Apply ADF test (null: unit root exists) AND KPSS test (null: stationary) jointly
- If ADF rejects but KPSS does not reject: stationary
- If both reject or neither rejects: fractionally differenced (see Marcos Lopez de Prado's approach)

**C. Volatility Normalization**
This is arguably the most important preprocessing step for financial ML.

```python
# Normalize returns by rolling volatility
normalized_return = return_t / rolling_std(returns, window=20)

# Or use GARCH-normalized returns
from arch import arch_model
garch = arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1)
result = garch.fit(disp='off')
standardized = returns / result.conditional_volatility
```

Why: A 1% move in gold during low-vol environments is a very different signal than 1% during high-vol. Without normalization, your LSTM learns a muddled mapping.

**D. Feature Scaling -- Walk-Forward Safe**

```python
# WRONG: fit scaler on entire dataset (look-ahead bias)
scaler.fit(all_data)

# CORRECT: fit scaler only on training window, transform test
scaler.fit(train_window)
train_scaled = scaler.transform(train_window)
test_scaled = scaler.transform(test_window)
```

Use `RobustScaler` (median/IQR) rather than `StandardScaler` (mean/std) -- financial data has fat tails and outliers that distort mean/std.

**E. Outlier Treatment**
- Winsorize at 3-sigma or use IQR-based capping
- Do NOT remove outliers -- they contain real market information (flash crashes, news events)
- Cap them to reduce undue influence on gradient updates

**F. Missing Data**
- Forward-fill is standard for financial data (last known price persists)
- Never interpolate -- it creates look-ahead bias
- Mark gaps explicitly (e.g., weekend gaps in forex with a binary feature)

**G. Feature Engineering -- Quant-Grade**

Essential features for LSTM input:

```
Returns:           log_return, abs_return (realized vol proxy)
Volatility:        ATR, Bollinger Band width, Garman-Klass vol, Parkinson vol
Momentum:          RSI(14), MACD, ROC(various periods)
Mean Reversion:    z-score of price vs moving average
Microstructure:    bid-ask spread (if available), volume profile
Calendar:          hour_of_day, day_of_week, month (cyclical encoding)
Cross-asset:       DXY for gold/forex, VIX for all, US10Y yield
Regime:            rolling Hurst exponent, rolling autocorrelation
```

---

## 4. Common Pitfalls in Financial ML

### Critical Errors (Will Invalidate Results)

| Pitfall | Description | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Look-ahead bias** | Using future information in training features or scaling | Strict temporal ordering; walk-forward only; no global normalization |
| **Information leakage in sequences** | Overlapping sequences where test sequences contain training data points | Ensure gap between train and test equal to sequence length |
| **Fitting on the full dataset** | Any preprocessing (PCA, feature selection, scaling) on full data | All fitting must occur within each walk-forward training window |
| **Overfitting to backtest** | Optimizing hyperparameters on the same data you report results on | Three-way split: train / validation / test; or nested walk-forward |
| **Survivorship bias** | Only including instruments that still exist | Less relevant for XAUUSD/EURUSD/BTCUSD specifically, but critical for stock universes |

### Methodological Errors (Will Produce Misleading Results)

| Pitfall | Description | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-stationarity ignored** | Training on raw prices | Use returns or stationary transformations |
| **Ignoring transaction costs** | Reporting gross returns | Model spread, commission, slippage explicitly; use realistic estimates (2-3 pips for EURUSD, $0.30-0.50 for gold, 0.1% for BTC) |
| **Ignoring market impact** | Assuming infinite liquidity | Not critical for small capital, but note it |
| **Regime non-stationarity** | Model trained in trending regime, tested in ranging | Include regime detection; report performance by regime |
| **Multiple testing bias** | Comparing 5 models and picking the best without correction | Apply Bonferroni or use Deflated Sharpe Ratio / PBO |
| **Sequence length sensitivity** | Arbitrarily choosing lookback window | Treat it as a hyperparameter; optimize via Optuna |
| **Target leakage via technical indicators** | Some indicators use future bars in their smoothing | Verify every indicator is causal (uses only past data) |

### Practical Errors (Will Cause Production Failures)

| Pitfall | Description |
|---|---|
| **Training/serving skew** | Feature computation differs between training and live inference |
| **Concept drift** | Model degrades as market dynamics change; must have retraining schedule |
| **Gradient issues** | LSTMs suffer from vanishing gradients on very long sequences; keep sequence length reasonable (50-200 for hourly, 30-90 for daily) |
| **Class imbalance** | If predicting direction, markets are roughly 50/50 but not exactly; use stratified sampling |

---

## 5. Returns vs Prices as Targets

### Definitive Answer: Use Log-Returns

**Never use raw prices as the prediction target.** Here is why:

| Criterion | Raw Prices | Simple Returns | Log Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stationarity | Non-stationary | Approximately stationary | Approximately stationary |
| Additivity | N/A | Not time-additive | Time-additive: sum of log returns = log return of period |
| Normality | Not normal | Approximately normal for short horizons | Slightly better normality properties |
| Symmetry | N/A | Asymmetric (-100% floor, no ceiling) | Symmetric |
| Small moves | N/A | r and ln(1+r) nearly identical | Equivalent for small moves |
| Compounding | N/A | Must be compounded multiplicatively | Sum directly for multi-period returns |
| Neural network training | Poor gradient behavior; scale changes over time | Good | Best |

### Practical Implementation

```python
# Target variable
log_return = np.log(close_t / close_{t-1})

# For multi-step ahead prediction (e.g., predict next 5 bars cumulative)
cumulative_log_return = np.log(close_{t+5} / close_t)
# This equals sum of individual log returns -- clean and additive

# Converting predictions back to prices
predicted_price = current_price * np.exp(predicted_log_return)
```

### When Simple Returns Are Acceptable

- For portfolio-level aggregation (cross-sectional returns of multiple assets are additive in simple return space, not log return space)
- When the audience/reporting requires it

### Classification Alternative

Many professional quant shops frame this as a classification problem:

```
Class +1:  next-bar log return > +threshold
Class  0:  abs(next-bar log return) <= threshold  (no-trade zone)
Class -1:  next-bar log return < -threshold
```

Where `threshold` is calibrated to transaction costs. This directly maps to a trading signal and avoids the problem of optimizing for point-estimate accuracy when all you need is direction.

---

## 6. Statistical Tests to Include

### Pre-Modeling Tests (Data Quality and Assumptions)

| Test | Null Hypothesis | Purpose | Library |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF)** | Series has unit root | Confirm returns are stationary | `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.adfuller` |
| **KPSS** | Series is stationary | Use jointly with ADF for robust conclusion | `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.kpss` |
| **Phillips-Perron** | Series has unit root | More robust to heteroskedasticity than ADF | `arch.unitroot.PhillipsPerron` |
| **Ljung-Box** | No autocorrelation up to lag k | Check if returns have predictable structure | `statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.acorr_ljungbox` |
| **ARCH-LM** | No ARCH effects | Confirm volatility clustering exists (justifies vol normalization) | `statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_arch` |
| **Jarque-Bera** | Returns are normally distributed | Quantify fat tails; will almost always reject for financial data | `scipy.stats.jarque_bera` |
| **Hurst Exponent** | H=0.5 (random walk) | H>0.5 suggests trending; H<0.5 suggests mean-reverting | Custom or `hurst` package |

### Model Evaluation Tests

| Test | Purpose | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Diebold-Mariano (DM)** | Compare predictive accuracy of two models | Pairwise comparison of your 5 model variants |
| **Model Confidence Set (MCS)** | Identify set of statistically equivalent best models | After running all 5 variants |
| **Giacomini-White** | Conditional predictive ability test; accounts for estimation uncertainty | More powerful than DM for nested models |
| **Mincer-Zarnowitz Regression** | Regress realized values on forecasts; test intercept=0, slope=1 | Forecast calibration check |
| **Pesaran-Timmermann (PT)** | Test directional accuracy | Is directional prediction better than chance? |

### Post-Modeling / Strategy Tests

| Test | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Bootstrap Sharpe Ratio CI** | Confidence interval on Sharpe; use circular block bootstrap to preserve autocorrelation |
| **Deflated Sharpe Ratio** | Adjusts for multiple comparisons across your 5 models |
| **White's Reality Check / SPA** | Tests if best strategy is significantly better than benchmark after data snooping adjustment |
| **CUSUM Test** | Detect structural breaks in model residuals over time |
| **Chow Test** | Test for regime breaks at known dates (e.g., COVID crash, rate hike cycles) |

---

## 7. Handling Market Regimes

### Why Regimes Matter

An LSTM trained predominantly in trending markets will fail catastrophically in ranging markets, and vice versa. Gold in 2020-2024 exhibited at least three distinct regimes (COVID flight-to-safety, post-COVID consolidation, 2024 breakout). BTCUSD has historically alternated between explosive trending and extended drawdown regimes.

### Regime Detection Methods

**A. Hidden Markov Models (HMM) -- Most Common in Quant Finance**

```python
from hmmlearn import GaussianHMM

# Fit 2-3 state HMM on returns + volatility
model = GaussianHMM(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", n_iter=100)
features = np.column_stack([returns, rolling_vol])
model.fit(features)
regimes = model.predict(features)
# States typically map to: low-vol trending, high-vol trending, ranging
```

**B. Rolling Hurst Exponent**

```
H > 0.6:  Trending regime  -> momentum strategies / trend-following signals
H ~ 0.5:  Random walk      -> reduce position size / go flat
H < 0.4:  Mean-reverting   -> mean-reversion signals
```

**C. Volatility Regime via GARCH or Simple Thresholds**

```
Low vol:    rolling_vol < 25th percentile of historical
Normal vol: 25th-75th percentile
High vol:   > 75th percentile
Crisis:     > 95th percentile
```

### Integration Strategies

**Option 1: Regime as Input Feature (Simplest)**
- Add regime label as a feature to LSTM input
- Model learns to condition predictions on regime
- Risk: regime detection itself may have lag

**Option 2: Regime-Specific Models (Most Robust)**
- Train separate LSTMs per regime
- Use regime detector as a routing layer
- Report performance per regime separately
- Challenge: less training data per regime

**Option 3: Regime-Aware Position Sizing (Pragmatic)**
- Single model for prediction
- Scale position size inversely with volatility regime
- Reduce or eliminate positions during regime transitions (high uncertainty)

**Option 4: Mixture of Experts**
- Train a gating network that learns to weight regime-specific expert models
- More complex but theoretically elegant

### Recommendation for Your Setup

Use Option 1 (regime as feature) combined with Option 3 (regime-aware sizing) and always report metrics broken down by regime in your results.

```
Overall Sharpe: 1.8
  - Trending regime:   2.4  (model excels)
  - Ranging regime:    0.9  (model struggles)
  - High-vol regime:   1.5  (adequate)
```

This level of transparency is what distinguishes professional quant reports from academic exercises.

---

## 8. What Makes a Financial ML Report Professional / Production-Grade

### Report Structure

```
1. Executive Summary
   - Strategy thesis in 2-3 sentences
   - Key metrics table (Sharpe, Max DD, Annual Return, Hit Ratio)
   - Investment recommendation

2. Data Description
   - Instruments, timeframes, date ranges
   - Data source and quality assessment
   - Summary statistics table (mean, std, skew, kurtosis, ADF p-value)
   - Return distribution plots with normal overlay

3. Feature Engineering
   - Complete feature list with economic rationale for each
   - Stationarity test results for all features
   - Correlation matrix / VIF for multicollinearity assessment

4. Methodology
   - Model architectures with layer dimensions
   - Walk-forward validation design (diagram)
   - Training protocol (optimizer, learning rate schedule, early stopping)
   - Hyperparameter optimization approach

5. Results
   - Per-model performance table (all metrics from Section 2)
   - Statistical significance tests (DM, MCS, Deflated Sharpe)
   - Equity curves with drawdown overlay
   - Performance by regime
   - Performance by year (vintage analysis)
   - Rolling Sharpe ratio plot (12-month window)
   - Monthly returns heatmap

6. Risk Analysis
   - Drawdown analysis (top 5 drawdowns with dates and recovery time)
   - VaR and CVaR at 95% and 99%
   - Stress test results (COVID crash, 2022 rate hikes, etc.)
   - Correlation with benchmark during stress periods

7. Robustness Checks
   - Sensitivity to hyperparameters
   - Performance with different lookback windows
   - Performance with perturbed entry/exit thresholds
   - Out-of-sample degradation analysis

8. Limitations and Risks
   - Known failure modes
   - Regime dependencies
   - Data limitations
   - Model decay expectations

9. Appendix
   - Full hyperparameter tables
   - All statistical test outputs
   - Code repository reference
```

### Visual Standards

| Chart | Purpose | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Cumulative returns vs buy-and-hold | Strategy value-add at a glance | matplotlib / plotly |
| Underwater (drawdown) plot | Risk visualization | QuantStats |
| Monthly returns heatmap | Seasonality and consistency | seaborn / QuantStats |
| Rolling 12M Sharpe | Performance stability over time | Custom |
| Predicted vs actual scatter | Forecast quality | matplotlib |
| Regime-colored equity curve | When the model works and when it does not | Custom |
| Feature importance / attention weights | Model interpretability | Custom |

### What Separates Amateur from Professional

| Amateur | Professional |
|---|---|
| Reports MSE only | Reports Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, max DD, hit ratio, profit factor |
| Single train/test split | Walk-forward with multiple windows |
| No transaction costs | Explicit cost modeling with realistic estimates |
| "Model achieves 95% accuracy" | "Directional accuracy of 54.2% (PT test p=0.003) with profit factor 1.67" |
| Cherry-picked backtest period | Full available history with regime breakdown |
| No statistical tests | DM test, Deflated Sharpe, bootstrap CIs |
| Gross returns | Net returns after costs, with sensitivity analysis on cost assumptions |
| No discussion of limitations | Frank assessment of when the model fails |
| Pretty charts | Informative charts with confidence bands |

---

## Summary Recommendations for Your Specific Setup

### Asset-Specific Considerations

**XAUUSD (Gold, 1H bars)**
- Highly sensitive to USD strength (DXY), real yields (TIPS), and risk sentiment (VIX)
- Include these as exogenous features
- Intraday seasonality matters -- London/NY session transitions drive volume
- Spread: approximately $0.30-0.50 per ounce

**EURUSD (Forex, 1H bars)**

- Include rate differential (ECB vs Fed), PMI surprises

### Walk-Forward Design

```
For 1H data (Gold, EURUSD):
  Training window:   2000-3000 bars (~3-4 months)
  Validation window:  500 bars (~3 weeks)
  Test window:        200-500 bars (~1-3 weeks)
  Step forward:       200-500 bars
  Total windows:      40-60+ for robust statistics

For Daily data (BTCUSD):
  Training window:   500-750 bars (~2-3 years)
  Validation window:  90 bars (~3 months)
  Test window:        60-90 bars (~2-3 months)
  Step forward:       60-90 bars
  Total windows:      10-15 (limited by BTC history)
```

### Model Comparison Protocol

1. Train all 5 architectures (Simple LSTM, Stacked LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, LSTM+Attention) under identical walk-forward protocol
2. Aggregate out-of-sample predictions across all windows
3. Compute all metrics on aggregated OOS predictions
4. Run pairwise Diebold-Mariano tests
5. Compute Model Confidence Set
6. Apply Deflated Sharpe Ratio to the winner
7. Report ALL models' results, not just the best one

### Final Caution

_PyTorch Forecasting_ is a PyTorch-based package for forecasting with state-of-the-art deep learning architectures. It provides a high-level API and uses [PyTorch Lightning](https://pytorch-lightning.readthedocs.io/) to scale training on GPU or CPU, with automatic logging.

---

Our article on [Towards Data Science](https://towardsdatascience.com/introducing-pytorch-forecasting-64de99b9ef46) introduces the package and provides background information.

PyTorch Forecasting aims to ease state-of-the-art timeseries forecasting with neural networks for real-world cases and research alike. The goal is to provide a high-level API with maximum flexibility for professionals and reasonable defaults for beginners.
Specifically, the package provides

- A timeseries dataset class which abstracts handling variable transformations, missing values,
  randomized subsampling, multiple history lengths, etc.
- A base model class which provides basic training of timeseries models along with logging in TensorBoard
  and generic visualizations such as actual vs predictions and dependency plots
- Multiple neural network architectures for timeseries forecasting that have been enhanced
  for real-world deployment and come with in-built interpretation capabilities
- Multi-horizon timeseries metrics

# Changelog

We do our best to avoid the introduction of breaking changes,
but cannot always guarantee backwards compatibility. Changes that may **break code which uses a previous release of Darts** are marked with a "🔴". Changes that deprecate functionalities are marked with a "🟠".

## [Unreleased](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/tree/master)

[Full Changelog](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/compare/0.43.0...master)

### For users of the library:

### For developers of the library:

## [0.43.0](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/tree/0.43.0) (2026-03-23)

### For users of the library:

**Improved**

- Improvements to data transformers:  [#3023](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3023) by [Krzsztof Pęczek](https://github.com/u8-krpeczek)
  - Added parameter `columns` to all data transformers (e.g. `Scaler`, `Diff`, `BoxCox`, ...) to apply the transformations only on subset of components. This makes it much easier to build multivariate pipelines where different components require different transformations.
- Improvements to `TFTExplainer` : [#3039](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3039) by [ReinerBRO](https://github.com/ReinerBRO).
  - `plot_variable_selection()` now returns the matplotlib figures for downstream usage (saving, editing, ...). It returns a single figure when explaining a single TimeSeries. Otherwise, it returns a list of figures.
  - `plot_variable_selection()` now accepts a `show_plot: bool = True` parameter that allows to suppress showing the plot.
  - 🔴 `plot_attention()` now also returns the matplotlib figures for all explained series, instead of only the matplotlib axis for the last series.

## [0.42.1](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/tree/0.42.1) (2026-03-07)

### For users of the library:

**Fixed**

- Removed an incorrect warning being raised by `NeuralForecastModel` regarding using static covariates with multivariate base models. [#3036](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3036) by [Dennis Bader](https://github.com/dennisbader).

## [0.42.0](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/tree/0.42.0) (2026-03-07)

### For users of the library:

**Improved**

- 🚀🚀 Added new forecasting model `NeuralForecastModel` to convert any of the **30+ NeuralForecast base models** into a Darts `TorchForecastingModel`. This includes models such as NBEATSx, PatchTST, TimeXer, KAN, and many more. Like all Darts torch models, it supports univariate, multivariate, probabilistic forecasting, optimized backtesting and more. Depending on the base model, it also supports past, future, and static covariates. [#3002](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3002) by [Zhihao Dai](https://github.com/daidahao)
  - Check out our new [NeuralForecastModel Notebook](https://unit8co.github.io/darts/examples/26-NeuralForecast-examples.html) for detailed examples. [#3026](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3026) by [Dennis Bader](https://github.com/dennisbader).
- 🚀🚀 Added **fine-tuning** support to all `TorchForecastingModel` and `FoundationModel` (such as `Chronos2Model` and `TimesFM2p5Model`) via the new `enable_finetuning` parameter. Supports full training, and partial fine-tuning by selectively freezing or unfreezing layers by name pattern. [#2964](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/issues/2964) by [Alain Gysi](https://github.com/Kurokabe).
  - Check out our new [Fine-Tuning Notebook](https://unit8co.github.io/darts/examples/27-Torch-and-Foundation-Model-Fine-Tuning-examples.html) for detailed examples.
- More fine-grained control over Reversible Instance Normalization for all torch models. Apart from the boolean trigger, parameter `use_reversible_instance_norm` now also supports setting the `RINorm` hyperparameters as a dictionary. [#3029](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3029) by [Zhihao Dai](https://github.com/daidahao).
- Created `darts.typing` module to collect typical type annotation in one place. Introduced `TimeIndex`, `TimeSeriesLike`, `TimeZone` type aliases for improved readability & maintainability of the code. Common type annotations can be added to this file in the future. [#3021](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3021) by [Michel Zeller](https://github.com/mizeller)

**Fixed**

- Disallowed `use_reversible_instance_norm=True` or `{"affine": True}` for foundation models to prevent checkpoint loading errors due to incompatible weights. [#3029](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3029) by [Zhihao Dai](https://github.com/daidahao).
- Updated the restrictive type hint for the timezone parameter `tz` to cover all timezone definitions supported by Pandas [tz_convert](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.DatetimeIndex.tz_convert.html). [#3015](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3015) and [#3035](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3035) by [Moritz Waldleben](https://github.com/mwaldleben).

**Dependencies**

- Removed the upper version cap on `scikit-learn<1.8.0` since `catboost` added support in version `1.2.10`. [#3025](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3025) by [Simon Michau](https://github.com/simonmichau).

### For developers of the library:

- Updated target-version to python310, and auto-refactored source code using ruff. [#3017](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/2589) by [Dennis Bader](https://github.com/dennisbader).
- Fixed all instances of [invalid-parameter-default](https://docs.astral.sh/ty/reference/rules/#invalid-parameter-default) errors. Improves type checker's ability to accurately reason about the code. [#3027](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3027) by [Michel Zeller](https://github.com/mizeller)

## [0.41.0](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/tree/0.41.0) (2026-02-10)

### For users of the library:

**Migration from PyPI "u8darts" package to "darts" package**

- The `darts` PyPI package now replaces `u8darts` with the same installation options (e.g. `darts`, `darts[torch]`, `darts[notorch]`, `darts[all]`). No code changes are required. See the [migration guide](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/blob/master/INSTALL.md#important-darts-pypi-package-changes-as-of-version-0410) for details.
  - If you have been using `darts` before: switch to `pip install "darts[torch]>=0.41.0"` and replace `darts` by `darts[torch]>=0.41.0` in your project requirements.
  - If you have been using `u8darts` before: switch to `pip install "darts>=0.41.0"` and replace `u8darts` by `darts>=0.41.0` in your project requirements.

**Improved**

- Improvements to forecasting models:
  - 🚀🚀 Added new forecasting model `TimesFM2p5Model`: Google's pre-trained 200M-parameter foundational model for zero-shot forecasting. It supports univariate, multivariate, and multiple time series forecasting without training and can output deterministic or probabilistic forecasts. [#2980](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/2980) by [Zhihao Dai](https://github.com/daidahao).
- Improvements to `TimeSeries` :
  - 🚀🚀 Added method `TimeSeries.plotly()` method for interactive time series visualization using Plotly backend. [#2977](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/2977) by [Dustin Brunner](https://github.com/brunnedu).
    - Provides interactive plotting with zoom, pan, hover tooltips, and legend interactions
    - Maintains API consistency with the existing `plot()` method for easy adoption
    - Supports deterministic and stochastic, univariate and multivariate series

"""
Recurrent Neural Networks
-------------------------
"""

import inspect
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections.abc import Sequence

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from darts import TimeSeries
from darts.logging import get_logger, raise_if_not, raise_log
from darts.models.forecasting.pl_forecasting_module import (
    PLForecastingModule,
    io_processor,
)
from darts.models.forecasting.torch_forecasting_model import DualCovariatesTorchModel
from darts.utils.data import ShiftedTorchTrainingDataset
from darts.utils.data.torch_datasets.utils import (
    PLModuleInput,
    TorchBatch,
    TorchTrainingSample,
)

logger = get_logger(__name__)


class CustomRNNModule(PLForecastingModule, ABC):
    def __init__(
        self,
        input_size: int,
        hidden_dim: int,
        num_layers: int,
        target_size: int,
        nr_params: int,
        dropout: float = 0.0,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        """This class allows to create custom RNN modules that can later be used with Darts' :class:`RNNModel`.
        It adds the backbone that is required to be used with Darts' :class:`TorchForecastingModel` and
        :class:`RNNModel`.

        To create a new module, subclass from :class:`CustomRNNModule` and:

        * Define the architecture in the module constructor (`__init__()`)

        * Add the `forward()` method and define the logic of your module's forward pass

        * Use the custom module class when creating a new :class:`RNNModel` with parameter `model`.

        You can use `darts.models.forecasting.rnn_model._RNNModule` as an example.

        Parameters
        ----------
        input_size
            The dimensionality of the input time series.
        hidden_dim
            The number of features in the hidden state `h` of the RNN module.
        num_layers
            The number of recurrent layers.
        target_size
            The dimensionality of the output time series.
        nr_params
            The number of parameters of the likelihood (or 1 if no likelihood is used).
        dropout
            The fraction of neurons that are dropped in all-but-last RNN layers.
        **kwargs
            all parameters required for :class:`darts.models.forecasting.pl_forecasting_module.PLForecastingModule`
            base class.
        """
        # RNNModule doesn't really need input and output_chunk_length for PLModule
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

        # Defining parameters
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.target_size = target_size
        self.nr_params = nr_params
        self.dropout = dropout

    @io_processor
    @abstractmethod
    def forward(
        self, x_in: PLModuleInput, h: torch.Tensor | None = None
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """RNN Module forward.

        Parameters
        ----------
        x_in
            Tuple of Tensors containing the features of the input sequence. The tuple has elements (past target,
            historic future covariates, future covariates, static covariates). The shape of the past target is
            `(batch_size, input_length, input_size)`.
        h
            Optionally, the hidden state.

        Returns

class _RNN_Backbone(Module):
    def __init__(self, cell, c_in, c_out, seq_len=None, hidden_size=100, n_layers=1, bias=True, rnn_dropout=0, bidirectional=False,
                 n_cat_embeds=None, cat_embed_dims=None, cat_padding_idxs=None, cat_pos=None, feature_extractor=None, init_weights=True):
        
        # Categorical embeddings
        if n_cat_embeds is not None:
            n_cat_embeds = listify(n_cat_embeds)
            if cat_embed_dims is None:  
                cat_embed_dims = [emb_sz_rule(s) for s in n_cat_embeds]
            self.to_cat_embed = MultiEmbedding(c_in, n_cat_embeds, cat_embed_dims=cat_embed_dims, cat_padding_idxs=cat_padding_idxs, 
                                               cat_pos=cat_pos)
            c_in = c_in + sum(cat_embed_dims) - len(n_cat_embeds)
        else:
            self.to_cat_embed = nn.Identity()
        
        # Feature extractor
        if feature_extractor:
            if isinstance(feature_extractor, nn.Module):  self.feature_extractor = feature_extractor
            else: self.feature_extractor = feature_extractor(c_in, seq_len)
            c_in, seq_len = output_size_calculator(self.feature_extractor, c_in, seq_len)
        else:
            self.feature_extractor = nn.Identity()
        
        # RNN layers
        rnn_layers = []
        if len(set(hidden_size)) == 1: 
            hidden_size = hidden_size[0]
            if n_layers == 1: rnn_dropout = 0
            rnn_layers.append(cell(c_in, hidden_size, num_layers=n_layers, bias=bias, batch_first=True, dropout=rnn_dropout, 
                                   bidirectional=bidirectional))
            rnn_layers.append(LSTMOutput()) # this selects just the output, and discards h_n, and c_n
        else: 
            for i in range(len(hidden_size)):
                input_size = c_in if i == 0 else hs * (1 + bidirectional)
                hs = hidden_size[i] 
                rnn_layers.append(cell(input_size, hs, num_layers=1, bias=bias, batch_first=True, bidirectional=bidirectional))
                rnn_layers.append(LSTMOutput()) # this selects just the output, and discards h_n, and c_n
                if rnn_dropout and i < len(hidden_size) - 1: 
                    rnn_layers.append(nn.Dropout(rnn_dropout)) # add dropout to all layers except last
        self.rnn = nn.Sequential(*rnn_layers)
        self.transpose = Transpose(-1, -2, contiguous=True)
        if init_weights: self.apply(self._weights_init) 

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.to_cat_embed(x)
        x = self.feature_extractor(x)
        x = self.transpose(x)                    # [batch_size x n_vars x seq_len] --> [batch_size x seq_len x n_vars]
        x = self.rnn(x)                          # [batch_size x seq_len x hidden_size * (1 + bidirectional)]
        x = self.transpose(x)                    # [batch_size x hidden_size * (1 + bidirectional) x seq_len]
        return x

        # by JUN KODA (https://www.kaggle.com/junkoda) in this notebook

# Comprehensive Library Comparison: Python Libraries for Financial Time Series Prediction with LSTM/Deep Learning

*Research conducted against live PyPI and GitHub data as of March 26, 2026. Your environment: PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124, RTX 3050 Ti Laptop GPU, 3.93 GB VRAM.*

---

## Your Project Context First

The assignment is **section 3b** of your CIDL project: "Time Series or Natural Language Processing application with LSTM." The grading criteria (25 points across 4 sub-items) rewards:

- Understanding of your problem and dataset (5 pts)
- Understanding of the models you built and how you trained them (5 pts)
- Experimental conditions, parameters, success criteria, results, interpretation (10 pts)
- Originality vs. copied source, what you changed (5 pts)

This directly shapes the library recommendation: **the professor wants evidence that you understand what is happening inside the model**, not just that you called a high-level API and got a number out.

---

## Category 1: Time Series Deep Learning Libraries

### 1. darts (Unit8)

| Property | Details |
|---|---|
| Version | 0.43.0 |
| Last Release | 2026-03-23 (released 3 days ago) |
| GitHub Stars | 9,284 |
| Maintenance | Extremely active - weekly releases in 2025-2026 |
| Python Requires | >= 3.10 |

**What it does.** darts is a unified time series library covering everything from ARIMA to Transformers to foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5). The `TimeSeries` object is the core abstraction - it handles datetime indices, covariates, and probabilistic forecasting uniformly.

**Models relevant to your use case:**
- `RNNModel(model="LSTM")` - vanilla unidirectional LSTM
- `RNNModel(model="GRU")` - GRU variant
- `BlockRNNModel(model="LSTM")` - block (encoder-decoder) LSTM
- `BlockRNNModel(model="GRU")` - GRU block variant
- `TFTModel` - Temporal Fusion Transformer (attention-based)
- `TransformerModel` - standard Transformer
- BiLSTM - **not natively supported as a string parameter**, but achievable via `CustomRNNModule` subclass with `bidirectional=True`

**Walk-forward validation.** darts has a first-class `historical_forecasts()` method that runs optimized expanding/sliding window backtesting. This is exactly walk-forward validation. You call it once and it handles all the windowing.

**Why useful for your project.** The pipeline abstraction (`Pipeline` class) handles the full `fit → transform → predict` cycle. Built-in metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE, R2. Professional visualization via both matplotlib and (as of v0.41) Plotly interactive plots.

**VRAM consideration.** The base `RNNModel` is lightweight. With `hidden_dim=128`, `n_rnn_layers=2`, `batch_size=32` on a sequence length of 60 timesteps, you will use under 500 MB VRAM. You have headroom to run multiple models sequentially.

**Key limitation for your project.** BiLSTM requires writing a custom subclass. Attention over LSTM output (the classic "LSTM + Bahdanau attention" pattern) is not available as a built-in - you have to implement it as a `CustomRNNModule`. This is actually a **pedagogical advantage** because it demonstrates understanding.

---

### 2. pytorch-forecasting (sktime org)

| Version | 1.6.1 |
| Last Release | 2026-01-23 |
| GitHub Stars | 4,847 (transferred to sktime org from jdb78) |
| Maintenance | Active - transferred to sktime org for long-term support |

**What it does.** Provides `TimeSeriesDataSet` for complex multi-series datasets with categorical embeddings, static covariates, and multi-horizon targets. Wraps PyTorch Lightning for training.

**Models relevant to your use case:**
- `RecurrentNetwork(cell_type="LSTM")` - LSTM with encoder-decoder structure
- `RecurrentNetwork(cell_type="GRU")` - GRU variant
- `TemporalFusionTransformer` - the flagship model, LSTM encoder + multi-head self-attention + gating
- `DeepAR` - probabilistic LSTM forecaster (Amazon research)
- `NBeats`, `NHiTS` - modern alternatives without RNN

**LSTM + Attention.** TFT is effectively an LSTM encoder with multi-head attention on top, which is close to your "LSTM+Attention" variant requirement. However, TFT is not "LSTM+Attention" in the clean academic sense - it is a full production-grade architecture that is harder to explain pedagogically.

**Key limitation for your project.** The `TimeSeriesDataSet` API has a steep learning curve. You must declare every feature as a static categorical, static continuous, time-varying categorical, or time-varying continuous variable. For a simple XAUUSD/EURUSD price series this overhead is disproportionate. The library also underwent a major refactor when moving to the sktime org, and documentation has gaps at v1.6.x.

### 3. tsai (fastai for time series)

**BiLSTM support.** This is the only high-level library where BiLSTM is a direct constructor parameter: `LSTMPlus(c_in, c_out, hidden_size=128, n_layers=2, bidirectional=True)`. The source code confirms `bidirectional=False` is a parameter on `_RNN_Backbone`. This directly matches your requirement.

**Why useful for your project.** `Learner` + `lr_find()` + `fit_one_cycle()` gives you state-of-the-art training with learning rate scheduling. The fastai `Learner` class provides `learn.recorder.plot_metrics()` for training curve plots out of the box.

**Key limitation.** The fastai abstraction hides training details. For a professor evaluating whether you understand LSTM internals, explaining fastai's `Learner` adds another layer of abstraction. **Why useful / not useful for your project.** GluonTS excels at probabilistic forecasting (confidence intervals, quantile outputs) and multi-series scenarios. For XAUUSD/EURUSD/BTCUSD as three separate series it works. However, simple LSTM models are not the focus - GluonTS pushes you toward DeepAR and Transformer architectures. **Verdict for your use case.** Not recommended as primary library. The learning curve is high and the library is not optimized for the "compare LSTM vs BiLSTM vs GRU" framing your project requires.

**Walk-forward validation.** `cross_validation()` method with `n_windows` parameter handles walk-forward natively.

**Why useful for your project.** This is actually the most "academically clean" high-level library for your comparison: you can do `NeuralForecast(models=[LSTM(...), GRU(...), NHITS(...)])` and run the same cross-validation on all three with identical data splits. ### The Recommendation: Hybrid Architecture

**The optimal approach for your CIDL project is raw PyTorch for the models + darts or NeuralForecast for the evaluation infrastructure.** Here is the rationale:

**Build the LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, and LSTM+Attention models from scratch in raw PyTorch.** This is approximately 80-150 lines of code per model using `nn.Module`. **What it does.** darts is a unified time series library covering everything from ARIMA to Transformers to foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5). The `TimeSeries` object is the core abstraction - it handles datetime indices, covariates, and probabilistic forecasting uniformly.

**Models relevant to your use case:**

- `RNNModel(model="GRU")` - GRU variant

- BiLSTM - **not natively supported as a string parameter**, but achievable via `CustomRNNModule` subclass with `bidirectional=True`

**Walk-forward validation.** darts has a first-class `historical_forecasts()` method that runs optimized expanding/sliding window backtesting. This is exactly walk-forward validation. You call it once and it handles all the windowing.

**Why useful for your project.** The pipeline abstraction (`Pipeline` class) handles the full `fit → transform → predict` cycle. Built-in metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE, R2. Professional visualization via both matplotlib and (as of v0.41) Plotly interactive plots.

**Key limitation for your project.** BiLSTM requires writing a custom subclass. Attention over LSTM output (the classic "LSTM + Bahdanau attention" pattern) is not available as a built-in - you have to implement it as a `CustomRNNModule`. ## The Critical Question: High-Level Library vs Raw PyTorch?

This is the most important decision for your project. Here is the rigorous analysis.

### Tradeoff Matrix

| Dimension | Raw PyTorch | darts | NeuralForecast | pytorch-forecasting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professor sees model internals | Full | Partial | Partial | Hidden |
| BiLSTM implementation | Manual | Custom subclass | Not available | Not available |
| Attention mechanism | Manual | Custom subclass | Not available | Via TFT only |
| Walk-forward validation | Manual loop | `historical_forecasts()` | `cross_validation()` | Manual |
| Professional metrics | Manual | Built-in | Built-in | Built-in |
| Setup complexity | Low | Medium | Low | High |
| VRAM efficiency control | Full | Partial | Partial | Low |
| Reproducibility (seeds) | Full | Partial | Full | Partial |
| Visualization quality | Manual | matplotlib/Plotly | matplotlib | matplotlib |
| Code you need to write | 400-600 lines | 150-250 lines | 100-200 lines | 200-350 lines |

### The Recommendation: Hybrid Architecture

**The optimal approach for your CIDL project is raw PyTorch for the models + darts or NeuralForecast for the evaluation infrastructure.** Here is the rationale:

**Build the LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, and LSTM+Attention models from scratch in raw PyTorch.** This is approximately 80-150 lines of code per model using `nn.Module`. You define the architecture explicitly - the professor can see that you understand what `bidirectional=True` does, how to implement Bahdanau attention as a separate module, and how to configure the hidden state dimensions.

**Use a utility library only for the non-model parts:**

- `yfinance` for data download
- `ta` or `pandas-ta` for technical indicator features
- `empyrical-reloaded` or `vectorbt` for trading performance metrics after predictions
- `tsfresh` optionally for advanced feature extraction

**Implement walk-forward validation manually** - this is approximately 30-50 lines and demonstrates understanding of temporal data leakage. The professor specifically grades "experimental conditions" for 10 points.

### Why Not darts as the Primary Tool?

darts is an excellent production library, but for your academic project it creates a specific problem: the `RNNModel` class abstracts away the PyTorch `nn.Module` entirely. When the professor asks "explain how your BiLSTM differs from your LSTM," you cannot point to code - you can only say "I passed `bidirectional=True` to a library class." That risks losing points on sub-item iv ("specify the differences between your work and that code").

However, darts is the right tool if you use it as a **comparison baseline**: "Here is our raw PyTorch LSTM achieving RMSE=X, and here is the darts built-in model achieving RMSE=Y, showing our implementation is competitive."

### Why Not NeuralForecast as the Primary Tool?

NeuralForecast is the cleanest high-level option and would be acceptable, but it has no BiLSTM and no LSTM+Attention. You cannot implement all four model variants the project requires without going to raw PyTorch anyway.

### The xLSTM Consideration

NeuralForecast 3.1.5 includes `xLSTM` and `xLSTMTime` (pytorch-forecasting also has it). Extended LSTM from the 2024 paper by Sepp Hochreiter's group addresses the "LSTM vs Transformer" scaling debate. If you want to add a fifth model variant that demonstrates current literature awareness, xLSTM is a strong choice and differentiates your project from standard assignments.
